semantic_reviews.coverage_confirmed: items_read: All 26 records in items_2.json: ITEM-6116-2-001 to 016, 018, 019, 020, 022, 023, P01 (12 MCQs with rationales), P02, P03. Every answer and marking line was checked against biology and the notes. notes_read: The whole of 2-classification-and-diversity-of-living-organisms.md. 2.1: key points, grouping, binomial, hierarchy, keys, connections. 2.2: key points, virus structure, viruses living, monocots, dicots, molluscs, annelids, insects, arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals, observing/drawing, connections. Also read: the topic 2 objective registry entries, MISCON-6116-030, and a grep of the exclusions and scope scan (no topic 2 exclusions). not_checked: Deterministic checks (arithmetic, references, coverage, scope, counts) and AO/Bloom/command-word/tariff labels were not checked, as the brief instructs. Flashcards not in the sample were not checked. Cross-reference targets (1.2.6, 3.8.3, topic 4) were not opened. The notes from other topics were not read.
semantic_reviews.reconstruction_test: q6_learner_test: OBJ-6116-2.1-04 (item 005, 4 marks), answered from the notes alone: 1a jointed legs absent -> A; 1b present -> 2; 2a antennae absent -> C; 2b antennae present -> 3; 3a one pair antennae -> B; 3b two pairs -> D. Earns 4/4, although the notes' own model couplet is weak (2-004). OBJ-6116-2.2-16 (item 022, 4 marks), answered from the notes alone: large continuous outline with no shading; ant drawn with head, thorax and abdomen in true proportion; ruled label lines ending on the parts; labels for three pairs of legs on the thorax, three body regions and one pair of antennae. Earns 4/4. Sampled flashcard-style items 001, 002, 009, 013, 015 and 020 can all be answered from the notes alone (for 020, wings is supported by 'Their forelimbs form the wings'). q7_misconceptions: Only ITEM-6116-2-023 carries a misconception_entry (MISCON-6116-030). It discriminates weakly. The learner must name the right group (crustacean) against the wrong one (insect), so it is more than a restated definition. But the stem's counts make the error obvious, and the arachnid side of the entry is not tested (2-010). The stem does not name the right group.

issues.finding: The Mammals section first states that all mammals have hair or fur at some stage of life, then says no single external feature is found in every mammal. Hair is an external feature, so the two sentences contradict each other. The whale example then says the whale "has some hair", which supports the first sentence and not the second.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner cannot tell whether hair is a defining mammal feature. They may hesitate to give hair as the diagnostic answer, or may repeat the "no single feature" line in an exam.
issues.recommended_repair: Delete "no single external feature is found in every mammal". Say instead that hair is present at some stage in every mammal, even if it is sparse, as in whales, and that limbs and habitat vary.
issues.resolution: Removed 'no single external feature is found in every mammal'. Notes now say every mammal has hair or fur at some stage; the whale has sparse hair; limbs and habitat vary. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The mammal features listed are hair/fur, mammary glands/milk and live birth. External ears (pinnae) and whiskers are missing. These are the standard visible external mammal features in Cambridge-style mark schemes for "list the visible external features used to classify mammals". Milk and live birth are not visible external features.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner asked for visible external features of a mammal has hair and nothing else visible to offer, and so loses the second mark.
issues.recommended_repair: Add external ears (pinnae) and whiskers as visible external features. Keep mammary glands, with a note that milk and live birth are not external.
issues.resolution: Mammal notes list the visible external features hair or fur, external ears (pinnae) and whiskers, and say milk and live birth are not visible external features. Item 015 also credits external ears. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The lion hierarchy ends with "species leo", which treats the specific name alone as the species. The section just before it says the specific name alone is not a complete species name, and item 004 marks the same point.
issues.educational_consequence: The learner meets two contradictory models. They may write "species = leo" in an answer about the binomial system and lose the mark.
issues.resolution: Lion hierarchy now ends 'species Panthera leo'. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

affected_ids: notes 2.1 Constructing and using dichotomous keys (worked example step 2)
issues.finding: In the worked key, step 2 pairs "body in ring-like segments" with "body with a shell". These are two unrelated features, not a contrasting pair (feature present / feature absent, or one state against another state of the same feature). The same notes require mutually exclusive choices, and item 005 gives a mark for "two contrasting statements". An animal with neither feature, such as a slug, has no route. An animal with both would have two routes.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who copies the model writes non-contrasting couplets and loses the contrasting-statement mark in key construction.
issues.recommended_repair: Change step 2 to "2a body divided into ring-like segments -> earthworm; 2b body not divided into segments -> snail" (or shell present / shell absent).
issues.resolution: Worked key step 2 is now 'body divided into ring-like segments' against 'body not divided into segments'. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The marking guidance first says feathers are "the one feature found only in birds". It then justifies the wings mark by saying wings "together with feathers" separate a bird from a bat. A bat has no feathers, so feathers alone already separate it from a bird. The stated reason for the second feature is invalid, and the prompt's "taken together, identify" premise rests on it. The notes also say "A bat has wings but no feathers, so feathers identify a bird."
issues.educational_consequence: The learner is trained to think a uniquely diagnostic feature still needs a second feature to rule out a group that lacks it. This muddles what diagnostic means.
issues.recommended_repair: Remove the bat clause and simply credit wings (or a beak with hard-shelled eggs, if wanted) as a supporting second feature. Alternatively, reword the prompt to "List two external features of a bird".
issues.resolution: Item 020 prompt is now 'List two visible external features of a bird.' The bat clause is gone; the second mark is for wings or a beak. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: A condition is dropped. P02(e)'s answer and the 2.1 notes say leg and antenna counts are fixed, or stay the same within a group. The 2.2 notes give crustaceans "more than four pairs" (crab 5, woodlouse 7) and myriapods "many". So leg count is fixed for insects and arachnids but not for every group. The 2.1 sentence is true in its insect context. P02(e)'s general claim ("stay the same within a group") is false.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner may reject a crustacean because its leg count differs from a crab's, or claim that every group has one fixed count.
issues.recommended_repair: Rephrase to "leg and antenna counts are structural features that fall in a set range for a group and differ between groups, whereas colour varies within a group".
issues.resolution: P02(e) answer and guidance now say leg and antenna counts fall in a set range for each group and differ between groups. The 2.1 notes no longer say the leg count is 'fixed'. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

affected_ids: notes 2.2 Observing and drawing local organisms
issues.finding: The objective says to concentrate on "diagnostic features and/or features that adapt them to their environment". The notes and item 022 cover only diagnostic features. The adaptation option is never mentioned and no example is given (for example, a thick waxy cuticle or a sunken stoma on a local desert plant).
issues.educational_consequence: A learner given a drawing task about adaptive features has no guidance on choosing or labelling them.
issues.recommended_repair: Add one sentence and one example on labelling adaptive features, for instance a succulent's swollen stem or a beetle's hard wing cases.
issues.resolution: Drawing notes now cover labelling adaptive features with their use (waxy cuticle of a desert plant, a beetle's hard wing cases). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The marking guidance accepts only dry scaly skin and leathery-shelled eggs laid on land. Eggs are not a visible external feature of the lizard. Clawed toes are given in the notes as a typical lizard feature that amphibians lack, but they earn no credit. Separately, the notes condition egg-laying with "most reptiles", which the item covers only through the word "typical".
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who correctly gives clawed toes from the notes loses the mark.
issues.recommended_repair: Add clawed toes (claws on the digits) to the creditable list.
issues.resolution: Item 019 now credits clawed toes as an alternative second feature. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The notes call gills the most dependable fish feature, but in bony fish the gills are hidden under the gill cover (operculum). Neither the operculum nor the lateral line, both standard visible features of fish, is mentioned.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner asked for visible external features has a smaller list to choose from, and may describe gills as directly visible.
issues.recommended_repair: Add "gill cover (operculum) over the gills" and "lateral line".
issues.resolution: Fish notes add the gill cover (operculum) and the lateral line. Item 011 credits both (gills or operculum count as one point). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The misconception entry is "crustaceans vs insects and arachnids". Item 023 tests only crustacean against insect, and the arachnid half is not tested. The stem gives both counts (five pairs of legs, two pairs of antennae), both well above the insect counts, so the error is obvious. The item asks the learner to recall counts. It does not make them choose between two plausible groups.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner can score full marks without being able to tell a crustacean from an arachnid. The near confusion, legs above four pairs against exactly four pairs, is never forced.
issues.recommended_repair: Add a case that sits close to the boundary, for example "a learner calls an animal with four pairs of legs and two pairs of antennae an arachnid", or ask for a three-way choice.
issues.resolution: Item 023 stem rewritten: the learner calls a 5-leg-pair, 2-antenna-pair animal an arachnid 'because it has more legs than an insect'. Marks are for naming the error (arachnids have four leg pairs and no antennae) and for the correct group, crustacean, with its features. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: P03 is mapped to OBJ-6116-2.2-16 (observe and draw), but nine of its ten marks test sampling design, means and bias. The topic 2 notes do not teach these. They need scientific-process content from topic 1 that the notes never cross-reference for sampling, only for drawing.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner revising topic 2 alone cannot prepare for most of this task.
issues.recommended_repair: Map P03 to the relevant 1.2 scientific-process objectives as well, or add a cross-reference from 2.2 to the sampling and variables content.
issues.resolution: Post-review repair: P03 no longer cites drawing objective OBJ-6116-2.2-16. It cites insect and crustacean identification objectives, and its final part now asks learners to identify both described animals. Generic sampling skills remain practical prerequisites. Author script and task regenerated; structural checks pass. This is an author resolution, not a second reviewer verdict.

issues.finding: The example of a realistic proportion, "an ant's abdomen drawn larger than its head", does not hold for every ant. Many ants, and soldier castes especially, have a head as large as the gaster or larger. The notes use a different comparison, abdomen against thorax.
issues.educational_consequence: A marker may penalise a faithful drawing of a large-headed ant, which is the very opposite of "draw what you see".
issues.recommended_repair: Change the marking to require proportions that match the specimen observed, and use the notes' abdomen-against-thorax example.
issues.resolution: Item 022 guidance now asks for proportions that match this specimen as observed, e.g. an ant's abdomen compared with its thorax. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

blockers: No deterministic opinion on 3 checks (C-35, C-41, C-43) - on these a human or model reviewer is the only line of defence.
notes: Standard v0.2.0-draft check suite. 44 checks: 40 pass, 0 fail, 1 warn, 3 not_run.
A not_run check means an input the check needs is absent. It is never a pass.
RS-30: these are mechanical results computed by code. They say nothing about whether the material teaches the subject well.
